newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia 1998 budget sees growth, lower deficit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia 1998 budget sees growth, lower deficit.

text.p: Russia's 1998 budget is betting on recovery after years of decline, a sharp drop in inflation and a continuing fall in government bond rates, a senior government source said on Tuesday.
A draft budget, to be submitted by the finance ministry to the cabinet on Thursday, assumes gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by two percent and industrial production by three percent in 1998.

"We consider the 1998 budget a budget for growth," said the source, who asked to remain anonymous. "Firstly we are lowering the tax burden on businesses and secondly we think we will be able to start a development budget."
Ministers had previously hoped recovery would set in this year but now their best hope is that output will be flat overall, although signs of growth have already re-appeared.
The Russian economy has been contracting since 1990, and by 1996 had fallen back to levels last seen in 1979, falling to only 61 percent of its size in 1991, the year the Soviet Union broke up.
On the other hand the rise in prices has been brought under control after a bout of hyperinflation in 1992.

The 1998 draft budget assumes an inflation rate of only five percent, less than half the 11.8 percent targeted for this year, which Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais acknowledged this month would be overshot.

The draft also plans a further reduction in the budget deficit, allowing yields on Treasury bills to fall further to 12-14 percent in 1998 from 18-19 percent currently and around 200 percent last year.
The budget deficit will be 132 trillion roubles ($22.7 billion), or 4.8 percent of GDP, down from a likely 5.35 percent of GDP this year, the source said.

The 1997 budget had originally planned a deficit of 3.5 percent but revenues at the start of the year were well below planned levels, forcing the government to cut spending. Revenues are planned next year at 340 trillion roubles and spending at 472 trillion.
Excluding debt servicing, the 1998 deficit will be only 0.42 percent.
Of the 1998 deficit, 102 trillion roubles will be financed domestically, and 30 trillion roubles will be borrowed abroad, including $3.5 billion in Eurobonds to be issued by Russia.

However, Russia may delay drawing some of its $10 billion three-year loan from the International Monetary Fund due next year until 1999, because of possible financing problems that year, the source said.

The delay, already agreed in principle by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, but to be discussed by the cabinet, would see drawings from the IMF's Extended Fund Facility of $2.0 billion in 1998 instead of a currently planned $2.6 billion, while drawings in 1999 would rise to $1.0 billion from $400 million.

The IMF, which over the past 12 months has repeatedly delayed payment of the loan because it was unhappy at the low level of Russian budgetary revenues, is now disbursing the loan on a quarterly basis after quarterly reviews of the economy.
The IMF board is due to meet on September 3 to consider the next disbursement, after an IMF mission left Russia earlier this month with generally favourable conclusions. ($ = 5,811 roubles)
